title: Butte at sunset, Face Canyon, Lake Powell, Utah, USA
desc: Hidden within an ancient sandstone landscape, Face Canyon is one of 96 canyons stretching out from Lake Powell in southern Utah. Many are far from roads and would be difficult to reach if they hadn't been flooded by the lake, which was created in 1963 during the construction of the Glen Canyon Dam. The lake's waters extend for around 186 miles (299 kilometres), along creeks and canyons which you can explore by boat, kayak or jet ski.

title: Rainbow Falls on the Wailuku River, Hilo, Hawaii, USA
desc: Water, sunlight and lush greenery come together at Rainbow Falls in Hilo, on the island of Hawaii. Here, the Wailuku River plunges around 24 metres over a lava ledge, sending mist into the air as it reaches the pool below. On sunny mornings, the mist can catch the light and produce the colourful rainbows that gave the falls their name. Known in Hawaiian as Waiānuenue, meaning 'rainbow water', this striking waterfall is surrounded by tropical vegetation and has a special place in Hawaiian legend.

title: Sunset Point, Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah, USA
desc: Snow transforms Bryce Canyon National Park, blanketing the landscape in white while its fiery orange-red hoodoos rise above the snowy terrain. Seen from Sunset Point, one of the park's best-known viewpoints, these fantastical shapes are part of the Claron Formation, a collection of sedimentary rocks deposited around 50 million years ago and later sculpted by weathering and erosion. Because much of the park lies above 2,440 metres, snow can arrive as early as October. In today's image, snow clings to the canyon's ridges and spires while mist drifts across the cliffs, creating an iconic winter scene in the American Southwest.

title: Red squirrel in Cairngorms National Park, Highlands, Scotland
desc: As Britain's only native squirrel species, red squirrels thrive in Scotland's Cairngorms National Park. An important refuge, the park offers ancient Caledonian pine forests and more recently planted conifer woodlands, providing valuable habitat and food for squirrels foraging for Scots pine seeds, nuts and other tasty morsels throughout the year. In today's image, a red squirrel is perched amid warm orange and yellow leaves, looking right at home as it ponders its next move in the Scottish Highlands.

title: Fiddlehead fern
desc: Today's image shows the gradual coiling of a young fiddlehead's tip, echoing the geometric patterns seen throughout nature. In maths, the Fibonacci sequence follows a similar progression, each number formed by adding the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and so on. Today is Fibonacci Day, chosen for the numbers of the date (11/23) to honour the sequence. Eventually the young fern frond shown here will unfurl as it grows, but elsewhere in the plant world, the sequence will continue to appear in the spiralling arrangements of sunflower heads, pinecones, succulents and pineapples.
main_text: The Fibonacci sequence was popularised through a 13th-century maths problem about multiplying rabbits.

title: The chapel and hermitage of Santa Justa in Cantabria, Spain
desc: Tucked into the rugged coastline of northern Spain, the 16th-century Hermitage of Santa Justa, featured in today's image, overlooks the crashing waves of the Cantabrian Sea. Built partly into the rock and associated with the relics of Saints Justa and Rufina, the small chapel eventually became a pilgrimage site. Its sheltered stone walls create a striking contrast with the powerful waves and rugged cliffs around it.

title: Nice, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France
desc: Bathed in a sun-kissed glow, Nice is a patchwork of terracotta rooftops, historic churches and pastel façades along the French Riviera, as seen in today's image. Founded by the ancient Greeks and long associated with the Italian House of Savoy, Nice officially became part of France in 1860. Today, its layered past remains visible throughout this coastal city in the south of France, where historic architecture meets the blue waters of the Mediterranean and the sunlit hills of the Côte d'Azur.

title: Diving humpback whale, Kvaloya, Troms, Northern Norway
desc: Off the coast of Kvaløya in Troms, northern Norway, humpback whales move through the cold Arctic waters in search of a proper feast. They visit the region in winter, following migrating herring into the fjords. Humpbacks are known for their remarkable feeding techniques, including bubble-net feeding, in which some whales blow rings or walls of bubbles to corral fish before surging upwards with their mouths open to catch their prey. In today's image, a humpback slips beneath the icy waves under a glowing pastel sky, capturing a moment of tranquillity in Norway's wild north.

title: The "Body of Knowledge" sculpture by Jaume Plensa at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany
desc: It's World Philosophy Day, when thinkers come together to explore life's enduring questions. To mark the occasion, today's image features "Body of Knowledge", a sculpture at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany. Created by Spanish artist Jaume Plensa, it combines steel letters from eight different alphabets to form a human figure. Plensa explains: 'Our body is the home of the spirit. The place in which ideas live.'

title: Pair of barn owls
desc: These barn owls, bathed in the evening light, are waiting for the hunt to begin. As night falls, the birds of prey swoop into action, listening for the faint movements of mice and voles in the grass and leaves. Their heart-shaped faces help funnel sound towards their exceptionally sensitive ears, allowing them to locate prey with remarkable precision in the dark. They then swoop down almost silently, their soft feathers helping to muffle the sound of their approach.
main_text: Barn owls don't hoot; they make eerie, screeching noises, which might explain their reputation as harbingers of doom.

title: Trail of the Cedars, Glacier National Park, Montana, USA
desc: Today's image features the Trail of the Cedars, one of 1,126 kilometres of hiking trails in Glacier National Park, Montana. Its 1.4km-long loop includes a raised boardwalk which cuts a path through western red cedars and hemlock trees. The park boasts routes for all abilities, taking in alpine lakes, wildflower meadows, mountain passes and wilderness stretching to the Canadian border.

title: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument, New Mexico, USA
desc: Incredible views and rock-solid foundations are part of the charm of these ancient dwellings, set into the cliffside in New Mexico. Nomads had long used the natural caves above Cliff Dweller Creek as temporary shelter, but it was the Native American Mogollon people who made them their home. Archaeologists believe they created dozens of rooms inside five alcoves in the 1270s and 1280s. Up to 15 families lived here at any one time, raising children, making pottery and overlooking the fertile Gila River valley where they grew crops and hunted wildlife. For reasons unknown, the Mogollon people moved on around 1300, leaving behind one of the American Southwest's most important archaeological sites.

title: Frozen azalea with red leaves
desc: As autumn's first frost sets in, ice crystals form on the leaves of evergreen shrubs, such as this azalea. The pinks, oranges and yellows of their spring blooms have long since faded, but a new colourful display awaits as their green leaves turn shades of red and purple. For the plants, these pigments can help protect leaves against environmental stresses as temperatures drop. For gardeners, they create a vibrant autumnal display, framed in white frost. When spring arrives, fresh green growth will emerge, and the colourful cycle begins anew.
main_text: The pigments that turn azalea leaves shades of red or purple are called anthocyanins.

title: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China
desc: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to more skyscrapers than any other city in the world. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters helped the island develop into a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth accelerated in the decades after the Second World War, fuelling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbour and the hills, developers had to build upwards, creating this distinctive skyline. As of 2026, Hong Kong has 569 completed buildings at least 150 metres tall — more than any other city in the world.

title: Abraham Lake in Alberta, Canada
desc: Dawn's first light reflects off the frozen surface of Abraham Lake, framed by the peaks of the Rocky Mountains. In winter, this picturesque lake in Alberta is famous for its frozen methane bubbles, trapped beneath the ice. Strong winds keep the ice largely clear of snow, revealing the bubbles below throughout the winter. As spring arrives and the ice thaws, the trapped gas can escape into the atmosphere.

title: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah, USA
desc: Just north of Moab, Utah, Arches National Park is home to more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches – the densest concentration of arches in the world. Today's image, North Window, is one of the best-known formations in the park's Windows Section, where towering fins, openings and sculpted sandstone create a landscape that looks almost architectural.

title: A field of poppies
desc: For Remembrance Day, we are looking out over a field of poppies, recognised as symbols of remembrance for more than a century.
main_text: The Poppy Appeal raised £56.6m in 2025 for work to support serving personnel, veterans and their families.

title: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
desc: From above, Rose Island looks like a brushstroke of green surrounded by every shade of blue. Just five kilometres east of Paradise Island in The Bahamas, this slender cay trades busy roads and city blocks for sandy shores, shallow waters and an inland lagoon. Its peaceful appearance comes with a touch of movie drama. Rose Island was used as a filming location for the 1965 James Bond adventure Thunderball, including the explosive destruction of the Disco Volante.

title: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
desc: Cross the Guadalquivir River in Seville, the capital of Spain's Andalusia region, and the city's rhythm seems to change. On the other side lies Triana, a colourful neighbourhood where ceramics, flamenco and local traditions are woven into everyday life. Since the 19th century, the Isabel II Bridge, also known as the Triana Bridge, has connected the neighbourhood to Seville's historic centre.

title: Lanterns for Diwali in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India
desc: What happens when the darkest night of the year gets the brightest celebration? Diwali. The Festival of Lights is celebrated by millions worldwide, bringing together diyas, lanterns, rangoli, prayers, sweets and family gatherings.

title: A bison in the grasslands of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, North Dakota, USA
desc: Bison are among the largest land mammals in the world, capable of weighing up to 900 kilograms and reaching speeds of 65 kilometres per hour despite their massive size. Despite often being called a buffalo, the American bison is not one of the true buffaloes, which are native to Africa and Asia. Its scientific name, Bison bison, leaves little room for confusion.

title: Bamboo forest, Pīpīwai Trail, Haleakalā National Park, Maui, Hawaii, USA
desc: A volcano, a rainforest and a bamboo grove? Haleakalā National Park on Maui has all three. Spanning Maui from its 3,055-metre summit to the coast, the park protects landscapes that change dramatically with elevation, rainfall and temperature. It was established in 1916 as part of Hawaii National Park and became its own national park in 1961. The name Haleakalā translates to 'House of the Sun', reflecting the Hawaiian mo'olelo of Māui capturing the Sun to lengthen the day.

title: Fireworks over Battersea Power Station, London
desc: Happy Bonfire Night, or Guy Fawkes Night, from London's iconic Battersea Power Station, which has towered over the Thames since the 1930s. Fireworks will be seen and heard across London and the UK tonight and over the weekend, to mark the anniversary of the 1605 Gunpowder Plot. The infamous bid to blow up the Houses of Parliament was foiled when Guy Fawkes was caught in the cellars, trying to light the fuse to hidden barrels of gunpowder. His name has since become synonymous with the plot, and his effigy has traditionally been burned to mark the date.

title: People rowing among colourful bald cypress, Xuancheng, Anhui, China
desc: People paddle through a glowing maze of bald cypress in Xuancheng, Anhui, where autumn transforms flooded woodlands into a tapestry of amber, copper and deep rust. Known scientifically as 'Taxodium distichum', bald cypress is unusual among conifers because it sheds its soft, feathery needles each fall, turning reddish-brown before they drop.

title: Lake Braies, Fanes‑Sennes‑Braies Nature Park, Dolomites, Italy
desc: Lake Braies sits almost 1,500 metres above sea level in the Dolomites of South Tyrol, northern Italy. Surrounded by forest and the dramatic peaks of the Fanes-Sennes-Braies Nature Park, the lake is known for its striking green and blue waters. A 3.5-kilometre trail circles the shore, while traditional wooden rowing boats offer another way to take in the scenery. The lake is also a starting point for several mountain walks, including the Dolomites' famous Alta Via 1.

title: Polar bear and cubs by Hudson Bay, Manitoba, Canada
desc: While November might bring us a step closer to the festive season, polar bears have other plans. They gather along the shores of Hudson Bay in Manitoba, Canada, waiting for sea ice to form so they can head back out to hunt seals. That annual spectacle inspired Polar Bear Week, observed during the first week of November, a celebration of the Arctic's largest land predator. Polar bears are powerful swimmers, expert hunters and remarkably adapted to life in one of Earth's harshest environments. Yet shrinking sea ice means many spend longer on land, making it harder to find food and raising the risk of encounters with people.
main_text: In a single season, a polar bear may cover more than 1,000 kilometres while searching for food and suitable ice.

title: Black Forest, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
desc: Today we're enjoying the misty views sweeping across the Black Forest, which stretches for around 160 kilometres across south-west Germany, bringing together wooded hills, deep valleys, lakes and charming towns. Its highest point, Feldberg, rises to 1,493 metres, while the Black Forest is also the starting point for the Danube and Neckar rivers. There's plenty of history and tradition here too. Forestry has long played an important role in the region, while its centuries-old clockmaking heritage helped make the distinctive cuckoo clock famous far beyond Germany.
